title: Leadership and Teamwork
description: Class 18 practice: leaders and managers, classic and contemporary leadership styles, the functions and principles of management, interprofessional collaboration, team communication (SBAR, read-back, handoffs), and team tools for safety and conflict.

questions.stem: A hospital names a staff nurse the new unit manager, with authority over scheduling, budgets, and hiring. A coworker asks what the new role means for the unit. Which statement by the charge nurse is accurate?
options: “She now holds a formal position, and she'll still need influence to lead us.”
“Her title gives her influence, so staff will follow her plans without persuasion.”
“She's now an informal leader, since her authority comes from her peers.”
“Managing is her job now, so leading the unit falls to the senior staff.”
questions.rationale:
A manager holds an official position in the organization, so management is always formal. Leadership is different: it's the use of interpersonal skills to influence others toward a goal. A new manager has authority, but still has to earn the staff's cooperation by leading.

“Her title gives her influence” is the tempting choice: authority and influence sound alike, but a title gives the right to direct, not the willingness to follow. An informal leader has no official appointment, which isn't the case here. And managing doesn't hand leading to someone else: every nurse, manager or not, is expected to lead.

Takeaway: Management is a formal position; leadership is influence. A good manager needs both.

questions.stem: During a busy night, a staff nurse with no charge role notices a new nurse falling behind, rallies two coworkers to help, and the unit runs smoothly. Coworkers often go to this nurse for advice. Which explanation fits this nurse's role best?
options: A formal leader acting on authority the unit gave her
A manager carrying out the organizing function for the shift
An informal leader whose influence comes from peers' trust
A charge nurse acting through the chain of command
questions.rationale:
An informal leader isn't appointed to direct others but takes on a leadership role because of who they are: coworkers trust the nurse, ask for advice, and follow when the nurse rallies them.

A manager organizing resources is the tempting choice, since the nurse did move people to where help was needed. But organizing is a management function, and management is always formal: this nurse holds no official position. A formal leader and a charge nurse both have official authority, which the stem rules out.

Takeaway: No title, but peers follow: that's an informal leader, leading by influence.

questions.stem: A nurse educator teaches a group of new graduate nurses about leadership and management. Which statement by a new graduate indicates an understanding of the teaching?
options: “I'll start building leadership skills once I'm ready for a charge role.”
“I'll lead and manage every shift, starting with my own clients' care.”
“A strong manager becomes a strong leader once the title brings respect.”
“My influence on the team will come mostly from my job title.”
questions.rationale:
All nurses manage and lead in practice: they manage their own clients' care, time, and resources, and they influence coworkers, clients, and families. So every nurse should keep building both skills from the first day.

Waiting for a charge role is the tempting choice, because leadership sounds like a job title. But leadership doesn't wait for a position. The other two choices tie influence to a title, which mixes up authority (from the position) with influence (from interpersonal skills).

Takeaway: Every nurse leads and manages, starting with their own clients; influence comes from skills, not a title.

questions.stem: A nurse manager and a respected staff nurse both want to shorten call-light response times on their unit. Which action should the nurse manager take, since it needs the manager's formal authority?
options: Share a vision of faster responses with coworkers
Model answering call lights promptly on each shift
Persuade peers to try a no-pass zone for call lights
Change the unit's assignments to add a float aide
questions.rationale:
Changing staff assignments and adding staff means directing others' work and assigning resources, which takes the authority of an official position: that's management.

Sharing a vision is the tempting choice, since managers do share visions. But a vision, role modeling, and persuasion are tools of leadership, and an informal leader can use all three without any title.

Takeaway: Influence (vision, example, persuasion) is open to any nurse; directing staff and resources takes a manager's formal authority.

questions.stem: A nurse manager is choosing a staff nurse to lead a falls-prevention project, and wants someone coworkers already follow. Which observations should the manager weigh in favor of a staff nurse?
options: Coworkers ask the nurse for advice on difficult cases.
The nurse has more years on the unit than anyone else.
Peers began a bedside safety check after the nurse modeled it.
The nurse explains goals in ways coworkers understand and accept.
The nurse holds the highest certification on the unit.
The nurse follows unit policies closely and rarely needs reminders.
questions.rationale:
Coworkers following a nurse is a sign of influence, the heart of leadership: peers ask the nurse for advice, copy what the nurse models, and accept the goals the nurse explains. An effective leader turns a vision into goals others understand, and acts as a role model.

Following policy closely is the tempting choice: it makes a reliable employee, but complying isn't the same as influencing others. Seniority and certification are worth respecting, but neither one shows that coworkers follow this nurse.

Takeaway: Look for influence (peers seek the nurse out, copy the nurse, accept the nurse's goals), not years, credentials, or compliance.

questions.stem: A nurse manager notices that staff follow a new hourly rounding policy only on the days she's on the unit. Which change in the manager's approach is most likely to make the practice last?
options: Explain why rounding matters and let nurses shape how it's done
Post the policy in the break room and audit rounding each week
Assign one nurse each shift to remind coworkers about rounding
Add rounding to each nurse's annual evaluation so it affects raises
questions.rationale:
Staff comply when the manager is watching because the policy rests on authority alone. Lasting change comes from leadership: a vision staff understand, and a say in how it's carried out, so they own the practice.

Weekly audits are the tempting choice: measuring is a real management function (controlling), and it can show the problem. But audits and evaluations tied to raises keep the practice tied to being watched or rewarded, and a reminder nurse just moves the watching to a coworker.

Takeaway: Authority gets compliance while someone's watching; vision and participation get commitment.

questions.stem: A charge nurse lets an experienced, motivated team decide among themselves how to divide the day's work, and checks in only when someone asks. Which leadership style is the charge nurse using?
options: Democratic
Laissez-faire
Bureaucratic
Situational
questions.rationale:
A laissez-faire leader takes a hands-off approach and lets the group decide based on its own expertise. It can work when the group is made up of committed, skilled members, like this team.

Democratic is the tempting choice, since the team does decide. But a democratic leader stays involved: the leader encourages discussion and coordinates the group's decision. A bureaucratic leader leads by the rules and procedures, and a situational leader adapts the style to each situation.

Takeaway: Hands-off, the group decides alone: laissez-faire. The leader guides a group decision: democratic.

questions.stem: A charge nurse usually asks for the team's input before making decisions. In which situation is the best choice for the charge nurse to make the decisions alone and give direct instructions?
options: Planning the unit's holiday schedule
Choosing a new bedside handoff format
Moving clients during a fire evacuation
Orienting experienced travel nurses to the unit
questions.rationale:
An autocratic leader makes the decisions and directs the activities. It's efficient and focused on the task, which is what an emergency like a fire needs: there's no time for discussion, and everyone must know exactly what to do.

Orienting experienced travel nurses is the tempting choice, since they're new to the unit. But they're experienced professionals, who do well with explanation and input, not orders. Holiday schedules and a handoff format affect the whole team and aren't urgent, so input builds commitment.

Takeaway: Emergencies and tasks with no time to discuss call for direct, autocratic leadership; otherwise, involve the team.

questions.stem: A nurse manager asks each shift for ideas on reducing falls, leads a discussion of the options, and has the staff choose one together. Which result should the manager plan for?
options: Quick decisions that follow a set protocol
Little need for the manager to coordinate
Close adherence to the existing procedures
More commitment, and a slower decision
questions.rationale:
This is democratic (participative) leadership: the leader encourages discussion and shared decision making, which builds engagement and productivity. Hearing from every shift takes coordination and time, so the decision comes more slowly.

Little need to coordinate is the tempting choice, since the staff make the choice. But a democratic leader stays involved and coordinates the group; a hands-off leader who doesn't coordinate is laissez-faire. Quick decisions fit an autocratic style, and adherence to procedures a bureaucratic one.

Takeaway: Democratic leadership trades speed for engagement, and needs a leader who coordinates.

questions.stem: Staff on a unit say their manager answers every suggestion with “That's not how the procedure reads,” even when a change would be safe and fit the unit's goals. Which problem is most likely to develop on the unit?
options: Dissatisfaction from the lack of flexibility
Confusion from a lack of clear procedures
Unsafe care from too little supervision of staff
Slow decisions from too many opinions
questions.rationale:
A bureaucratic leader works strictly within the organization's policies and procedures and allows little flexibility, which can leave staff dissatisfied.

Unsafe care from too little supervision is the tempting choice, because the manager isn't responsive to staff. But this manager supervises closely, by the rules: too little supervision is the risk of a laissez-faire style. Unclear procedures is the opposite of this unit's problem, and slow decisions from many opinions fits a democratic style.

Takeaway: Rules first, little flexibility: bureaucratic leadership, with dissatisfied staff as its risk.

questions.stem: A charge nurse leads two experienced nurses and a new graduate. Midmorning, a client on the unit suddenly deteriorates. Which approach should the charge nurse take with the team today?
options: Let the three nurses organize their own work, as the experienced ones prefer
Direct the team during the emergency, and coach the new graduate closely
Hold a quick team vote before each decision so everyone shares it
Follow the unit's written routine exactly so the new graduate learns it
questions.rationale:
A situational leader adapts the style to the situation and the people: direct leadership while a client is deteriorating, and more guidance for a new graduate than for experienced nurses. Flexibility is the key.

Letting all three organize their own work is the tempting choice: it fits the experienced nurses, but it leaves the new graduate without support and the emergency without direction. A vote is too slow for an emergency, and following the written routine exactly is rigid when the situation has changed.

Takeaway: Match the style to the moment and the person: direct in a crisis, coaching for a novice, hands-off for experts on a routine day.

questions.stem: A charge nurse usually involves the team in decisions. In which situations should the charge nurse give direct instructions instead of asking the team for input?
options: Choosing the theme for the unit's practice council meeting
A client on the unit goes into cardiac arrest
Planning next month's staff education topics
A smoke alarm sounds and the unit must evacuate
A new nurse's client has a falling oxygen saturation
Deciding which shift tries a new break schedule first
questions.rationale:
Direct, autocratic leadership fits emergencies and situations where someone needs clear direction right away: a cardiac arrest, an evacuation, and a new nurse with a client whose oxygen saturation is falling (the novice needs direction, and the client can't wait).

The break schedule is the tempting choice, since someone has to decide it. But it isn't urgent, and the people affected have useful input, so involving them builds commitment. The council theme and education topics are also good chances for participation.

Takeaway: Urgent and safety-critical, or a novice who needs direction: give direct instructions. Not urgent: involve the team.

questions.stem: A nurse manager's hands-off style worked well with the unit's long-time, skilled staff. After half the staff are replaced by new graduates, missed tasks and near misses increase. Which action should the nurse manager take first?
options: Keep the hands-off style so the new nurses build independence
Ask the staff to vote on how the unit should be led
Give more direction and structure as the new nurses learn
Write a stricter procedure manual and have each nurse sign it
questions.rationale:
A laissez-faire style works only when the group is skilled and committed. The group has changed, and the near misses show it, so the leader adapts (situational leadership): more direction and structure until the new nurses have the skills to work more independently.

A stricter manual is the tempting choice, since it adds structure. But a rule-based (bureaucratic) fix gives new nurses paperwork, not the direction and coaching they need, and it costs flexibility. Keeping the hands-off style ignores the near misses, and a vote on leadership doesn't help nurses who don't know the work yet.

Takeaway: Hands-off leadership fits experts. When the team changes, the leader's style changes with it.

questions.stem: A nursing student says, “Some people are born leaders, and I'm just not one of them.” Which response by the nurse educator is accurate?
options: “That's often true, since leadership traits are mostly set by adulthood.”
“Leadership comes with a formal title, so you'll learn it once you're promoted.”
“Leaders need a charismatic personality, so focus on your clinical skills.”
“Leadership styles develop through education, training, and experience.”
questions.rationale:
Behavior-based theories hold that leaders develop their style through education, training, and experience, so leadership can be learned.

Leadership traits set by adulthood is the tempting choice: it matches the oldest, trait-based theory (leaders are born with certain traits), which is exactly what the student believes. The class presents behavior-based and later theories, which say leadership is learned. Leadership also doesn't wait for a title, and charisma is one contemporary style, not a requirement.

Takeaway: Trait theory says leaders are born; behavior theory says they're made, through education, training, and experience.

questions.stem: A nurse manager shares a vision of a restraint-free unit, coaches each nurse on alternatives, and asks staff to come up with creative solutions. Staff go well beyond what's required. Which leadership style does the manager's approach fit best?
options: Transformational
Transactional
Charismatic
Laissez-faire
questions.rationale:
A transformational leader motivates the group toward a shared vision, coaches each person (individual consideration), encourages creative problem solving (intellectual stimulation), and often gets performance beyond what's expected.

Charismatic is the tempting choice, since the manager inspires staff. But a charismatic leader engages the group through personality, while this manager builds the vision, coaches, and asks staff to solve the problem. A transactional leader exchanges rewards for meeting expectations, and a laissez-faire leader steps back.

Takeaway: Vision, coaching, creative problem solving, and results beyond expectations: transformational.

questions.stem: A nurse manager gives staff an extra day off when the unit meets its hand-hygiene audit goal, and corrects nurses when an audit shows a missed step. Which result should the manager expect from this approach?
options: Performance far beyond what's expected
Results that match the expected targets
Little direction, since the manager steps back
Strong loyalty to the manager's personality
questions.rationale:
This is transactional leadership: rewards in exchange for meeting set goals (contingent reward), and correcting errors when monitoring finds them (management by exception). It tends to produce expected outcomes.

Performance far beyond what's expected is the tempting choice, since rewards motivate. But going beyond expectations is the mark of transformational leadership, which motivates through a shared vision rather than an exchange. Stepping back is laissez-faire, and loyalty to a personality is charismatic.

Takeaway: Transactional leadership gets the expected results; transformational leadership gets more than expected.

questions.stem: A nurse manager's unit has high staff turnover and burnout, and a rising number of medication errors. Based on the leadership research from class, which approach should the nurse manager work to develop?
options: Passive leadership, giving staff more independence
Transactional leadership, linking rewards to the audit results
Transformational leadership, coaching toward a shared goal
Bureaucratic leadership, tightening the unit's procedures
questions.rationale:
Research on nursing leadership links transformational leadership with better staff well-being, higher job satisfaction, less burnout, and a lower intention to leave, and with client outcomes like fewer medication errors and higher satisfaction. That matches all three of this unit's problems.

Transactional leadership is the tempting choice: rewards tied to audits can bring error numbers up to target. But it produces expected outcomes, not the retention and well-being this unit needs. Passive (avoidant) leadership is linked to poorer outcomes, and tighter procedures can add to dissatisfaction.

Takeaway: Turnover, burnout, and safety problems point to transformational leadership, the style the research favors.

questions.stem: A charge nurse starts each shift by asking every nurse, “What do you need from me to care for your clients today?” She removes obstacles and helps staff grow, and staff say they feel empowered. Which leadership style is the charge nurse using?
options: Transactional
Autocratic
Charismatic
Servant
questions.rationale:
A servant leader puts the needs of the team first, supports and develops them, and uses strong communication skills; as followers grow, they feel empowered to act in the best interests of the organization and the people around them.

Charismatic is the tempting choice, because staff respond well to this charge nurse. But a charismatic leader engages people through personality, not by serving their needs. A transactional leader trades rewards for results, and an autocratic leader makes the decisions and directs.

Takeaway: “What do you need from me?” is the servant leader's question: serve and develop the team, and the team is empowered.

questions.stem: On a unit's practice council, nurses, a pharmacist, and a physical therapist each lead the agenda items in their own area, and decisions are made together. Which benefit should the unit expect from this structure?
options: Broader decisions that draw on each member's expertise
Faster decisions, since one leader sets the whole direction
Fewer meetings, since members act independently
Clearer authority, through a single chain of command
questions.rationale:
Shared leadership builds on collective action: leadership moves among members, so decisions draw on more people's expertise, a broader decision-making process.

Clearer authority through one chain of command is the tempting choice, since a council is a formal structure. But shared leadership spreads leadership across members rather than concentrating it. One leader setting the direction is the opposite of shared leadership, and members who act independently aren't sharing decisions.

Takeaway: Shared leadership spreads leading across the team, for broader decisions built on everyone's expertise.

questions.stem: A nurse manager wants to lower turnover and help staff perform beyond expectations. Which actions should the nurse manager take?
options: Meet with each nurse about goals and offer coaching
Rely mainly on bonuses for meeting audit targets
Share a clear picture of what the unit could become
Step back and let staff handle problems on their own
Invite staff to find creative solutions to unit problems
Act with integrity and keep commitments to staff
questions.rationale:
These are the parts of transformational leadership, the style linked to lower turnover and performance beyond expectations: coaching each nurse (individual consideration), an inspiring vision (inspirational motivation), creative problem solving (intellectual stimulation), and integrity that builds trust (idealized influence).

Bonuses for audit targets is the tempting choice, since rewards do motivate. But rewards in exchange for meeting targets are transactional, and produce expected results, not results beyond them. Stepping back is a passive, laissez-faire approach, linked to poorer outcomes when the team needs leadership.

Takeaway: Vision, coaching, creativity, and integrity are the four parts of transformational leadership.

questions.stem: Staff at a nursing home say the director of nursing is rarely seen on the units and acts only after a problem becomes serious. Staff turnover is high. Which explanation of this leadership is best supported by the research from class?
options: A hands-off style that works because the staff are experienced
A passive, avoidant style linked to poorer outcomes for staff
A transactional style that corrects errors after they happen
A bureaucratic style focused mainly on the facility's rules
questions.rationale:
Acting only once problems become serious, and being largely absent, is passive-avoidant leadership: passive management by exception and laissez-faire, an absence of leadership. Research found this style far too common in nursing homes, and linked it to poorer leadership outcomes, while transformational leadership is linked to staying on the job.

Transactional correction of errors is the tempting choice, since the director does react to problems. But a transactional leader monitors actively and corrects errors as they're found; this director waits until problems are serious. A hands-off style that works needs a committed, stable team, and the high turnover says this one isn't working.

Takeaway: Active monitoring and correction is transactional; waiting until problems are serious is passive-avoidant, the style linked to the worst outcomes.

questions.stem: A nurse manager compares the unit's monthly fall rate with the target set in January, and gives staff feedback on the results. Which management function is the manager carrying out?
options: Planning
Organizing
Controlling
Coordinating
questions.rationale:
Controlling uses measures to monitor and evaluate progress toward goals: setting a performance standard, comparing actual results with it, and giving feedback.

Planning is the tempting choice, since a target was involved. But setting the target in January was planning; comparing this month's results with it is controlling. Organizing assigns staff, equipment, and supplies, and coordinating (directing) motivates people and delegates work.

Takeaway: Set the goal: planning. Measure results against it and give feedback: controlling.

questions.stem: Before flu season, a nurse manager writes a staffing plan to put in place if more than a fifth of the staff call out sick at once. Which kind of plan has the manager written?
options: A strategic plan
An operational plan
A budget plan
A contingency plan
questions.rationale:
A contingency plan prepares for something that may happen, based on how likely it is, like a wave of staff illness during flu season.

A strategic plan is the tempting choice, since it's also prepared in advance. But a strategic plan sets the organization's long-term outcomes, usually through a committee that gathers data from stakeholders over months. An operational plan carries out day-to-day work, and a budget plans spending.

Takeaway: “If this happens, we'll do that” is a contingency plan; long-term organizational goals are a strategic plan.

questions.stem: The hospital has approved four new beds on a unit. The nurse manager works out which staff, equipment, and supplies will go to the new beds, and who will report to whom. Which management function is the manager carrying out?
options: Organizing
Controlling
Coordinating
Planning
questions.rationale:
Organizing is identifying and assigning resources, from staff to equipment and supplies, and setting out who reports to whom in the structure.

Planning is the tempting choice, since it all happens before the beds open. But the decision to add the beds was the plan; arranging the people and things to carry it out is organizing. Controlling measures results against standards, and coordinating motivates people and delegates work as it's done.

Takeaway: Deciding the goal and the course of action is planning; lining up the staff, equipment, and structure to do it is organizing.

questions.stem: At the start of a shift, the charge nurse explains the day's goals to the team, delegates tasks to the assistive personnel, and encourages everyone to keep each other updated. Which management function is the charge nurse carrying out?
options: Organizing
Coordinating
Controlling
Planning
questions.rationale:
Coordinating (directing) uses communication to motivate the group and move the work forward, and delegation is part of it.

Organizing is the tempting choice, since assignments are involved. But organizing identifies and assigns resources; here the charge nurse is communicating, motivating, and handing off tasks as the work begins, which is directing. Controlling measures results, and planning sets the goals.

Takeaway: Communicating, motivating, and delegating while the work goes on is coordinating (directing).

questions.stem: A hospital's leaders want to improve the hospital's nursing outcomes over the next five years. Which step should the leaders take first?
options: Have the chief nursing officer write the plan and announce it
Have each unit manager set its own goals for the year
Form a committee that gathers data from stakeholders
Have the staff vote on the goal at a staff meeting
questions.rationale:
This is a strategic plan: it focuses on the organization's outcomes. Planning starts from assessment data, and a strategic plan usually involves a committee working over several months to gather and analyze data from stakeholders.

Having the chief nursing officer write the plan is the tempting choice, since leaders are responsible for the strategy. But writing it before gathering data skips the assessment that planning is built on, and leaves out the stakeholders. Unit goals are short-term and fragmented, and a vote chooses a goal without the data to support it.

Takeaway: Planning starts with assessment data; a strategic plan comes from a committee gathering data from stakeholders.

questions.stem: A nurse manager's unit has a goal of cutting central line infections in half this year. Which actions should the nurse manager take to find out whether the unit is meeting the goal?
options: Order more central line dressing kits
Set a monthly infection rate as the standard
Assign a nurse to each line-care task
Compare each month's rate with the standard
Give staff feedback on the results
Draft next year's budget for supplies
questions.rationale:
Finding out whether a goal is being met is controlling: set a performance standard, compare actual results with it, and give feedback.

Ordering more dressing kits is the tempting choice, since supplies help prevent infections. But that's organizing resources; it doesn't tell the manager whether the goal is being met. Assigning tasks is directing, and next year's budget is planning.

Takeaway: Controlling is a loop: a standard, a comparison with real results, and feedback.

questions.stem: A new nurse asks the preceptor how being accountable differs from being responsible. Which statement by the preceptor matches the definitions from class?
options: “You're responsible to your scope of practice, and accountable for your duties.”
“They mean the same thing in nursing, though managers use them differently.”
“Managers are accountable for outcomes, while staff nurses are responsible for tasks.”
“You're accountable to your scope of practice, and responsible for your duties.”
questions.rationale:
In the class's definitions, a nurse is accountable to something, like the scope of practice, and responsible for carrying out their professional roles and duties.

The first choice is the tempting one: it uses the same two pieces with the words swapped. Accountable to the standard, responsible for the work. The two terms aren't the same, and both apply to every nurse, not just to managers or just to staff.

Takeaway: Accountable to (the scope of practice); responsible for (your duties).

questions.stem: A charge nurse asks a staff nurse to take the next admission. The staff nurse says, “You're a nurse just like me. You can't tell me what to do.” Which statement about the charge nurse's authority is accurate?
options: The facility gives the charge role the right to direct others' work
Authority comes from seniority, so it depends on years of service
The charge nurse can direct the assistive personnel, but not nurses
Assigning admissions belongs to the nurse manager, not the charge nurse
questions.rationale:
Authority is the right to direct others and their activities to reach outcomes. It comes from the organization: the facility gives the charge role that right, in line with its chain of command.

Authority from seniority is the tempting choice, since experienced nurses often have influence. But influence and authority are different: authority comes with the position, not the years. A charge nurse directs nurses as well as assistive personnel, and making assignments during the shift is part of the role.

Takeaway: Authority comes from the position the organization gives; influence comes from the person.

questions.stem: Two nurses on a unit have argued about lunch breaks for weeks, and coworkers have started taking sides. Which action should the nurse manager take first?
options: Schedule the two nurses on different shifts for the next month
Meet with both nurses to hear each side and agree on a plan
Write a break policy and post it for the whole unit
Refer both nurses to the employee assistance program
questions.rationale:
Managing conflict is one of a manager's principles, and conflict on a team affects everyone. The first step is to bring the two nurses together, hear each side, and reach an agreement on next steps, which keeps the conflict healthy and resolves it at its source.

Writing a break policy is the tempting choice, since it addresses the topic. But a policy imposed without talking to the people in conflict leaves the conflict itself unresolved. Separating the nurses avoids it, and the employee assistance program may help later, but it hands off a work problem the manager should address first.

Takeaway: Address conflict directly with the people involved, before rules, reassignments, or referrals.

questions.stem: Halfway through the year, a nurse manager sees that the unit's supply spending is well above the projected budget. Which action should the nurse manager take?
options: Reduce the float staff hours to balance the budget
Ask staff to borrow supplies from other units
Review where costs differ from the projection and adjust
Request a larger budget for next year and keep spending as is
questions.rationale:
Managing resources means knowing how the budget affects care, and adapting when actual expenses differ from the projected ones. So the manager finds out where and why costs differ, and changes practices to match best practice.

Cutting float staff hours is the tempting choice, since it balances the numbers quickly. But it takes from staffing, which affects safe care, to fix a supply problem it doesn't explain. Borrowing supplies moves the cost elsewhere, and asking for more next year doesn't manage this year's spending.

Takeaway: When actual costs differ from the budget, find the cause and adjust; don't fix one resource by cutting another.

questions.stem: A nurse manager wants to improve staff engagement and the unit's outcome measures. Which actions should the nurse manager take?
options: Involve staff in choosing how to improve a quality measure
Make unit decisions herself so staff can focus on care
Help each team member understand the group's purpose
Address conflicts between staff members early
Wait for staff to ask for help before stepping in
Plan the workday so time goes to the top priorities
questions.rationale:
The principles of management include enhancing performance through staff engagement and participation, building teams whose members understand the group's purpose, managing conflict, and managing time.

Making decisions herself so staff can focus on care is the tempting choice, since it sounds considerate. But it takes away the participation that builds engagement and improves outcome measures. Waiting for staff to ask for help is passive: problems grow before the manager acts.

Takeaway: Engage staff, build the team around a shared purpose, address conflict early, and manage time.

questions.stem: A hospitalist asks a cardiologist to see a client and advise on managing the client's new atrial fibrillation. The hospitalist stays in charge of the client's care. Which kind of request has the hospitalist made?
options: A transfer of care
A referral
A handoff
A consultation
questions.rationale:
In a consultation, one provider formally asks another for input or advice on how to approach or treat a condition, and keeps managing the client.

A referral is the tempting choice, since the terms are often used interchangeably. But in a referral, the provider hands responsibility for managing the condition to the other provider. A transfer of care turns all of the client's care over to another provider, and a handoff passes information and responsibility at a shift change or transition.

Takeaway: Consult: advice, and the first provider stays in charge. Referral: the condition's management moves. Transfer: all care moves.

questions.stem: A client's primary care provider sends the client to a wound specialist, who will now manage the client's foot ulcer, while the primary care provider keeps managing the client's other conditions. A family member asks the nurse what happened. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Your mother has been referred to the specialist for her ulcer.”
“The specialist is consulting, so your mother's provider decides.”
“Your mother's care has been transferred to the specialist.”
“The specialist will advise, and her provider will treat the ulcer.”
questions.rationale:
In a referral, one provider gives another the responsibility for managing a specific condition: the specialist now manages the ulcer, and the primary care provider keeps the rest.

“Transferred” is the tempting choice, since the ulcer's care moved. But a transfer of care turns over all of the client's care, and here the primary care provider still manages the other conditions. A consultation (the second and fourth choices) means the specialist only advises, while the first provider keeps managing the condition.

Takeaway: One condition's management moves to another provider: referral. Everything moves: transfer. Advice only: consultation.

questions.stem: A hospital's error reviews keep finding that nurses, pharmacists, and therapists each knew part of a problem, but no one put the pieces together. Which change should the hospital's education council make?
options: Train each discipline separately on its own procedures
Train the disciplines in shared classes and drills
Write more detailed safety policies for each department
Make the provider the single decision maker for care
questions.rationale:
Health professionals educated in silos, only within their own discipline, is one of the things that keeps medical errors going. Training the disciplines together builds the shared understanding and communication that interprofessional teams need.

More detailed department policies is the tempting choice, since policies feel like a safety fix. But they strengthen the silos instead of connecting them. Separate training is the silo itself, and a single decision maker loses what each discipline brings.

Takeaway: Errors that fall between disciplines call for interprofessional education and teamwork, not more silos.

questions.stem: A hospital is building an interprofessional education program on the Interprofessional Education Collaborative (IPEC) core competency areas. Which areas should the program cover?
options: Roles and responsibilities
Discipline-specific skills checkoffs
Values and ethics for interprofessional practice
Teams and teamwork
Billing for each discipline's services
Interprofessional communication
questions.rationale:
IPEC's core competency has four areas: values and ethics for interprofessional practice, roles and responsibilities, interprofessional communication, and teams and teamwork.

Discipline-specific skills checkoffs is the tempting choice, since every team member needs skills. But checkoffs within one discipline are silo training, not interprofessional competency. Billing isn't part of the competency.

Takeaway: IPEC's four areas: values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork.

questions.stem: A client recovering from a stroke wants to go home and walk to the mailbox. The nurse, physical therapist, occupational therapist, and dietitian each have their own plan, and the plans don't line up. Which action by the nurse best supports collaborative care?
options: Follow the nursing plan and let each discipline follow its own
Ask the provider to decide which discipline's plan comes first
Suggest a team meeting, with the client, to set shared goals
Email the nursing plan to the other disciplines to review
questions.rationale:
Collaborative care is client-centered: the disciplines come together, bring their knowledge and skills, and work toward a common goal with the client, who is always part of the team.

Emailing the nursing plan is the tempting choice, since it shares information. But it's one-way, and it doesn't make the goals shared. Following separate plans is working in silos, and asking the provider to pick one plan loses the other disciplines' expertise and the client's voice.

Takeaway: Collaboration means one set of goals, built together, with the client at the table.

questions.stem: A provider calls a nurse with a telephone prescription for a new medication for a client. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Repeat it aloud to the provider, then write it in the record later
Ask the provider to text the prescription to the unit's phone
Write it down, and confirm it with the provider at morning rounds
Write it down, read it back as written, and get the provider's OK
questions.rationale:
For a telephone prescription, the nurse records it, reads it back exactly as written to the prescriber, and gets the prescriber's verification (receive, record, read back).

Repeating it aloud is the tempting choice: it sounds like a read-back. But the class's rule is to read back what you wrote, not repeat what you heard, since the error can happen in the writing. Confirming at rounds leaves an unverified prescription in the meantime, and a text is not how prescriptions are received.

Takeaway: Record, read back from what you wrote, verify: don't just repeat it.

questions.stem: A nurse calls a provider about a client who had a hip replacement this morning, using SBAR. Which statement should the nurse make for the Assessment part of the call?
options: “I'm concerned she may be bleeding internally.”
“She had a right hip replacement at 8 this morning.”
“I'm calling about Ms. Lane in room 4, who looks pale.”
“I'd like you to see her and order a hemoglobin.”
questions.rationale:
In SBAR, the Assessment is what the nurse thinks the problem is, with the findings that support it: here, a concern about bleeding.

The surgery this morning is the tempting choice, because it's what makes bleeding likely. But that's Background, the clinical context. “I'm calling about Ms. Lane, who looks pale” is the Situation (what's going on), and asking the provider to come and order a test is the Recommendation or request.

Takeaway: Situation: what's going on. Background: the context. Assessment: what I think the problem is. Recommendation: what I'd like done.

questions.stem: During an I-PASS handoff, the receiving nurse has heard the client's illness severity, summary, and action list, and the situation awareness and contingency plans. Which action should the receiving nurse take next?
options: Thank the nurse and go do the first assessment
Summarize the report back and restate the to-do items
Read the chart to check the information that was given
Ask the charge nurse to confirm the illness severity
questions.rationale:
The last step of I-PASS is Synthesis by the receiver: the receiving nurse summarizes what was heard, asks questions, and restates the key actions and to-do items. It closes the loop, so errors are caught before the giving nurse leaves.

Reading the chart is the tempting choice, since checking information is good practice. But it doesn't give the giving nurse a chance to correct a misunderstanding, and it comes after the handoff, not in place of its last step. Leaving to assess skips the synthesis, and the illness severity was already given.

Takeaway: A handoff isn't finished until the receiver summarizes it back and asks questions.

questions.stem: During a rapid response, the nurse sees the client's oxygen saturation drop to 84%. The team leader is at the head of the bed giving instructions. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Record the value on the flowsheet for the team leader to see
Tell the nearest team member quietly, so the team isn't distracted
Say the value aloud to the whole team, directed to the leader
Wait until the team leader asks for the latest vital signs
questions.rationale:
A call-out communicates critical information to all team members at once during an emergency, so everyone can anticipate the next steps, and it directs the information to the person responsible for acting on it.

Telling one team member quietly is the tempting choice, since it seems courteous not to interrupt. But in an emergency, the whole team, and above all the leader, needs the information now. Charting it and waiting to be asked both delay a critical finding.

Takeaway: Critical information in an emergency is called out: aloud, to everyone, directed to the person who acts on it.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes teaching a client how to use a new inhaler at home. Which action should the nurse take to best confirm that the teaching was clear?
options: Ask, “Do you have any questions about the inhaler?”
Ask the client to repeat the steps back word for word
Give the client a printed handout to review at home
Ask the client to explain its use in their own words
questions.rationale:
A teach-back confirms that the nurse explained the information clearly: the client explains what to know or do in their own words.

Repeating the steps word for word is the tempting choice, since it sounds thorough. But repeating can be done from memory without understanding, while explaining in one's own words shows it. Asking whether the client has questions invites a “no” that confirms nothing, and a handout supports teaching but doesn't check it.

Takeaway: Teach-back: the client explains it in their own words. Check-back: a team member repeats a message to the sender.

questions.stem: A nurse is giving a shift handoff report on a client. Which elements should the nurse include to make the handoff complete?
options: Clear, specific information about the client
A written note in place of a spoken report
Acknowledgment by the receiving nurse
Transfer of responsibility for the client
A brief summary given while heading to another room
Time for the receiving nurse to ask questions
questions.rationale:
A proper handoff transfers responsibility and accountability, gives clear information, is spoken, is acknowledged by the receiver, and leaves time for questions and review.

A written note is the tempting choice, since writing seems more precise. But handoffs are given verbally, so the receiver can acknowledge and ask questions; a note can support a report, not replace it. A summary given in passing leaves no time for questions, and interruptions during handoffs are a known cause of errors.

Takeaway: A complete handoff is spoken, clear, acknowledged, and open to questions, and it transfers responsibility.

questions.stem: During an emergency, a provider says, “Give furosemide 40 mg IV now.” The nurse replies, “Furosemide 40 mg IV now.” Which response from the provider completes the exchange?
options: “That's correct.”
“Go ahead and give it.”
“Call me with the urine output.”
“Document it as a verbal order.”
questions.rationale:
A check-back is closed-loop communication: the sender gives the message, the receiver repeats it, and the sender confirms that it was heard correctly. The provider's “That's correct” closes the loop.

“Go ahead and give it” is the tempting choice: it sounds like approval. But it doesn't confirm that the dose, drug, and route the nurse repeated are right. The other two are reasonable next instructions that also skip the confirmation.

Takeaway: A check-back has three parts: the sender says it, the receiver repeats it, and the sender confirms it.

questions.stem: During this morning's handoff, the day nurse told a new graduate, in front of the client, “I can't believe you didn't get this client's weight.” The new graduate wants to resolve the conflict. Which statement is the best way for the new graduate to start?
options: “You're too hard on new nurses, and it's hurting the whole team.”
“Earlier, you raised the missed weight where the client could hear.”
“I'll get the weight tonight, so let's not bring it up again.”
“Let's ask the charge nurse which shift should do the weights.”
questions.rationale:
The DESC script for conflict starts by Describing the specific situation or behavior with concrete facts. Then the nurse Expresses the concern, Suggests alternatives, and states the Consequences for the client and the team's goals.

Asking the charge nurse is the tempting choice: it fixes the workflow question. But it skips talking with the coworker directly and leaves the way the comment was made unresolved. A judgment like “too hard on new nurses” is about the person, not a specific behavior, and promising to drop it avoids the conflict.

Takeaway: DESC: Describe (facts), Express (concern), Suggest (alternatives), Consequences (for the client and team).

questions.stem: Before surgery, a nurse tells the surgeon that the sedated client's consent form lists the left knee, but the surgeon is marking the right knee. The surgeon keeps marking without answering. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Call the nursing supervisor to the room right away
Note the concern in the client's record and continue the setup
Restate the concern firmly and ask for acknowledgment
Wait for the time-out to bring up the concern again
questions.rationale:
The two-challenge rule: when a first assertive statement is ignored, the nurse is responsible for restating the concern, and the person challenged must acknowledge hearing it. If the concern still isn't resolved, the nurse takes stronger action, involves other team members, and uses the supervisor or the chain of command.

Calling the supervisor right away is the tempting choice: it is part of the rule, but it comes after the second challenge. Waiting for the time-out gives the error more time, and noting the concern and continuing lets a possible wrong-site surgery go ahead.

Takeaway: Challenge twice; if the concern is still ignored, go up the chain of command. Anyone can stop the line for safety.

questions.stem: A nurse thinks a client with a new oxygen requirement isn't safe to discharge today. The nurse's first concern was brushed aside by the provider. Which statement should the nurse make next?
options: “I'm a little worried about the discharge plan.”
“Could we think again about the discharge plan?”
“I'm uncomfortable with it, but it's your decision to make.”
“This is a safety issue. I can't support the discharge.”
questions.rationale:
CUS gives assertive statements in rising order: “I'm Concerned,” “I'm Uncomfortable,” and “This is a Safety issue.” After a concern is brushed aside, the nurse moves up to naming the safety issue, which signals that the plan should stop.

“I'm uncomfortable” is the tempting choice, since it's the next step up. But ending with “it's your decision” takes the challenge back. The first two choices repeat the level of concern that was already dismissed.

Takeaway: CUS climbs from Concerned to Uncomfortable to Safety issue; “safety issue” means stop and address it.

questions.stem: A charge nurse wants the team to talk about what went well and what to change after a rapid response on the unit. When is the best time for this session?
options: Soon after the event, in a short, structured talk
At the start of the next shift, during the brief
During the event, as soon as the client is stable
At the next monthly staff meeting, with the manager
questions.rationale:
A debrief is a short, structured, informal exchange soon after an event, to improve the team's performance through lessons learned and to reinforce what went well.

The next shift's brief is the tempting choice, since it's a team meeting. But a brief shares the plan before work starts, and many of the people involved won't be there. During the event is the time for a huddle, to adjust the plan, and a monthly meeting is too late for details to be fresh.

Takeaway: Brief before (share the plan), huddle during (adjust it), debrief after (learn from it).

questions.stem: A charge nurse sees a new nurse skip the two-identifier check while giving a client's medication. Which features should the charge nurse's feedback have?
options: Given soon after the missed check
Focused on the behavior, not the nurse's character
Saved for the new nurse's annual evaluation
Specific about the step that was missed
Linked to how the missed step could affect the client
Noting what the new nurse did well
Given in front of the team as a teaching moment
questions.rationale:
Formative feedback improves team performance. It's timely (soon after the behavior), respectful (about behaviors, not personal attributes), specific, directed toward improvement, appreciative (it notes what the nurse does well), considerate, and client focused (how the behavior affects the client).

Giving it in front of the team is the tempting choice, since others could learn too. But feedback is considerate: correction in front of coworkers isn't, and it makes the nurse defensive. Saving it for the annual evaluation loses the timeliness that makes feedback work.

Takeaway: Good feedback is timely, specific, respectful, appreciative, considerate, and client focused.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that a coworker, on her third double shift this week, has twice nearly hung the wrong IV bag this shift. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Report the near misses to the nurse manager after the shift
Point out the near misses and offer to double-check her IVs
Fill out an incident report on both near misses before leaving
Suggest that the coworker ask for fewer double shifts next week
questions.rationale:
Cross-monitoring and mutual support mean watching each other's back: noticing a teammate's fatigue and workload (the I'M SAFE checklist), and offering help right away, so mistakes are caught before they reach a client.

The incident report is the tempting choice: near misses should be reported, but reporting can wait until the client is safe, and it doesn't protect this shift's clients. Telling the manager after the shift also leaves the rest of the shift unprotected, and fewer shifts next week doesn't help today.

Takeaway: When a teammate is at risk of error, back them up now; report and fix the system after the clients are safe.
